{{Short description|Smallest ordinal number that, considered as a set, is uncountable}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''first uncountable ordinal''', traditionally denoted by <math>\omega_1</math> or sometimes by <math>\Omega</math>, is the smallest [[ordinal number]] that is the [[order type]] of an [[uncountable]] [[well-ordered set]]. It is the [[supremum]] (least upper bound) of all countable ordinals. In the [[von Neumann ordinal|von Neumann representation]], the elements of <math>\omega_1</math> are the countable ordinals (including finite ordinals),<ref>{{Cite web|title=Set Theory > Basic Set Theory (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)|url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/set-theory/basic-set-theory.html|access-date=2020-08-12|website=plato.stanford.edu}}</ref> of which there are uncountably many.

The [[cardinality]] of the set <math>\omega_1</math> is the first uncountable [[cardinal number]], <math>\aleph_1</math> ([[aleph-one]]). The ordinal <math>\omega_1</math> is thus the [[Ordinal number#Initial ordinal of a cardinal|initial ordinal]] of {{tmath|\aleph_1}}. Like all other initial ordinals of infinite cardinals, <math>\omega_1</math> is a [[limit ordinal]], i.e. there is no ordinal <math>\alpha</math> such that {{tmath|1=\omega_1 = \alpha+1}}. Formally, cardinal numbers are usually represented as their initial ordinals, in which case <math>\omega_1</math> and <math>\aleph_1</math> are considered equal as sets. More generally, for any ordinal {{tmath|\alpha}}, <math>\omega_\alpha</math> denotes the initial ordinal of the cardinal {{tmath|\aleph_\alpha}}.

The [[continuum hypothesis]] (CH) states that {{tmath|1=\beth_1 = \aleph_1}} (where {{tmath|1=\beth_1 = 2 ^ {\aleph_0} = \vert \mathbb{R} \vert}} is the second [[beth number]]), which implies that {{tmath|1=\vert \omega_1 \vert = \vert \mathbb{R} \vert}}, i.e., the countable ordinals are [[equinumerous]] to the [[real number]]s. If CH does not hold, but the [[axiom of choice]] (AC) does, then {{tmath|\vert \omega_1 \vert}}, as the smallest uncountable cardinal, is strictly less than {{tmath|\vert \mathbb{R} \vert}}. If AC also does not hold then {{tmath|\vert \omega_1 \vert}} may be [[Comparability|incomparable]] with {{tmath|\vert \mathbb{R} \vert}}, but never larger than {{tmath|\vert \mathbb{R} \vert}}.<ref>{{Cite web|title=first uncountable ordinal in nLab|url=https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/first+uncountable+ordinal|access-date=2020-08-12|website=ncatlab.org|archive-date=2020-10-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201003023350/https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/first+uncountable+ordinal|url-status=live}}</ref>

The existence of <math>\omega_1</math> does not depend on AC, as it can be constructed explicitly as the [[Hartogs number]] of {{tmath|1=\omega_0 = \mathbb{N} }}. More concretely, the set of all well-orderings on {{tmath|\mathbb{N} }} can be constructed as a subset of all binary relations on {{tmath|\mathbb{N} }}, and thus applying the [[axiom of replacement]] to replace every well-ordering with its order type will give {{tmath|\omega_1}}.

== Topological properties ==
Any ordinal number can be turned into a [[topological space]] by using the [[order topology]]. When viewed as a topological space, <math>\omega_1</math> is often written as <math>[0,\omega_1)</math>, to emphasize that it is the space consisting of all ordinals smaller than <math>\omega_1</math>.

If the [[axiom of countable choice]] holds, every [[sequence|increasing &omega;-sequence]] of elements of <math>[0,\omega_1]</math> converges to a [[Limit of a sequence|limit]] in <math>[0,\omega_1]</math>. The reason is that the [[union (set theory)|union]] (i.e., supremum) of every countable set of countable ordinals is another countable ordinal.

The topological space <math>[0,\omega_1)</math> is [[sequentially compact]], but not [[compact space|compact]]. As a consequence, it is not [[metrizable space|metrizable]]. It is, however, [[countably compact space|countably compact]] and thus not [[Lindelöf space|Lindelöf]] (a countably compact space is compact if and only if it is Lindelöf). In terms of [[axioms of countability]], <math>[0,\omega_1)</math> is [[first-countable space|first-countable]], but neither [[separable space|separable]] nor [[second-countable space|second-countable]]. 

The space <math>[0,\omega_1]=\omega_1 + 1</math> is compact and not first-countable. <math>\omega_1</math> is used to define the [[long line (topology)|long line]] and the [[Tychonoff plank]]—two important counterexamples in [[topology]].
